title: Microsoft Teams to get AI protection against phishing and fraud
summary: Microsoft is adding a new AI-powered security feature to Teams aimed at detecting phishing, scams, and identity theft by analyzing conversations, Bleeping Computer reports. Instead of primarily checking for malicious links and files, the tool will be able to identify suspicious behavior in the messages themselves, Microsoft said. The feature will primarily be used for new contacts, as they pose a higher security risk. The new security feature follows earlier warnings from Microsoft about attackers impersonating help desk staff in Teams to trick users into granting them remote access. In a Microsoft 365 Message Center post ( mirror ), the company said, “During initial quality validation, detection may run in the background without showing warnings to users. After validation, users may see a warning when potential phishing is detected.” According to Microsoft, no messages will be saved or used to train AI models. The tool will also be used solely for security purposes — not, for example, for surveillance or advertising. The rollout will begin in early November 2026 and is expected to be generally available during the first half of December. IT teams do not have to configure the feature; it will be automatically enabled. This story originally appeared on Computer Sweden . Related: New malware turns Microsoft 365 and Azure into its control center Video: How modern work is creating a cybersecurity nightmare

title: Apple’s triple-whammy week begins with iPad mini
summary: Apple watchers predicted something like this: The company is ending October with a triple-whammy of new products, starting with its newly introduced iPad mini with OLED display. The rest of the week is expected to feature new Macs, specifically an M6 MacBook Pro and iMac and Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro. There’s no disputing how popular the iPad mini has become among some business users. Professionals use it as a digital notebook, many use it as a second display for their Mac, and some industries, particularly logistics, hospitality and field services, make extensive use of these things. If you want something smaller and lighter than a full-weight iPad, the iPad mini fills the gap, though its high build-quality means it comes at a price — starting at $699 with 128GB storage. That’s up from the $599 price tag on the previous model. Thanks to RAMaggedon, it’s the second price hike so far this year: two years ago, the device held a $499 starting price. The new 256GB model costs $799, while the 512GB iteration sets you back $999. A fully specified 512GB iPad mini with Wi-Fi, cellular, and nano-texture glass costs $1,249. What’s new in the iPad mini? Apple has focused deeply on making the new iPad mini thinner and lighter than before. (Here’s what I I thought about the previous model when I reviewed it.) The new iteration is 5.4mm thick, compared to 6.3mm, and weighs 0.58 pounds, in contrast to the previous model’s 0.66 pounds. It has a large 8.5 inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches), but this fits in the same footprint thanks to thinner bezels. The move to OLED means it delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous generation. Apple promises pixel-level lighting control for much deeper blacks and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vivid and accurate images. The display also weaves in some additional tech: Apple calls it an “Acoustic Display” because it has placed specially designed woofers and tweeters

title: Technology has changed. So should the conversation.
summary: I’ve spent more than 20 years talking about technology and how it can improve people’s lives. For most of that time, I was optimistic about the future. I still believe tech can make our lives better. But I’m increasingly concerned that companies building technology have stopped asking whether it actually does. I think it’s time we started asking harder questions. My column for Network World (2000-2018) aimed to explain the benefits of new devices and software to business and personal users. This same optimism carried over to my podcasting and video career, where Today in Tech (on Computerworld) and DEMO (on CIO.com) continued the technology conversation with industry thought leaders. Somewhere along the way, the relationship between technology companies and their customers changed. The tech industry now seems more interested in telling us what we need than listening to what we want. New technologies are being pushed into our workplaces, devices, and daily lives, often without clear explanations of how they make things better. Often, there are hidden benefits for the tech companies themselves (personal data, algorithms that exploit users’ emotions, etc.) We’re expected to embrace the future simply because the companies building it tell us we should. This goes well beyond AI, although it’s certainly accelerating the problem. Technology now shapes how we work, communicate, consume information (both real and fake), and understand the world around us. Social media has changed political discourse. Algorithms compete for our attention. Increasingly, decisions made by a handful of technology companies (and the billionaires who run them) affect millions of people who have no say in those decisions. I now believe that technology has become too important to leave the conversation entirely to the companies building and selling it. title: Oracle adds a semantic layer to ground AI agents in the business context
summary: Oracle is expanding its Autonomous AI Lakehouse with a Business Semantic Layer designed to give AI agents a consistent understanding of enterprise data, a move aimed at improving the accuracy of AI-generated insights and helping organizations scale agentic applications across business functions. To ground AI agents in business context, the Business Semantic Layer uses catalog annotations, SQL annotations imported from Oracle AI Database, and AI-suggested analytic views to create reusable models of enterprise data that capture dimensions, measures, hierarchies, calculations, and key performance indicators (KPIs), Oracle said in a statement. These models can then be used across Oracle’s natural-language querying, data retrieval, and analytics capabilities, including Select AI, to help ensure that queries and insights are based on consistent business definitions. Oracle said that the new capabilities will be available within the next 12 months. Alongside the new layer, at the company’s annual AI World conference, Oracle also launched a Business Simulation Engine to help enterprises evaluate business scenarios and make more informed planning decisions by integrating Oracle Essbase into the Autonomous AI Lakehouse. Beyond forecasting and what-if analysis, the engine supports write-back, dynamic hierarchy rollups, advanced calculations, and allocations, the company said. Enterprise users can also ask questions in natural language, generate simulation reports, and perform Excel-based analysis on data stored in Oracle databases or in object storage via the new engine, it added. Additionally, Oracle is expanding Apache Iceberg support in the lakehouse to let customers create, populate, update, and delete Iceberg tables using SQL, while improving performance and functionality when accessing Iceberg data through external catalogs or its AI Data Catalog. title: How malicious downloads can trick AI coding agents into compromising themselves
summary: Malicious instruction files planted in a computer’s Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into executing harmful code or exposing authentication tokens, Forever Security said after blocking an attempted attack on a customer’s machine and demonstrating similar techniques against OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code. In its research report, the firm said it discovered a malicious AGENTS.md file in a customer’s Downloads folder that instructed Codex to install a malicious npm package called function-color. The installation was blocked before the malware could execute. The researchers could not determine how the original file reached the computer, but demonstrated that a malicious website could trigger a similar download without a separate approval prompt. The attack exploits the way AI coding assistants process project-specific instructions. Codex uses AGENTS.md, while Claude Code supports CLAUDE.md. Both can interpret instructions contained in these Markdown files when operating in directories where the files are present. The attack requires the agent to operate in the affected directory and process the malicious file. For Codex, the directory must also be trusted, according to Forever Security. In tests using the file recovered from the customer’s machine, Forever Security found that Codex could be manipulated into modifying its machine-wide MCP server configuration and launching another session with approval and sandbox restrictions bypassed. Codex followed the malicious instructions in more than 90% of tests, most of which used a harmless substitute for the malware. Because the malicious server was registered in Codex’s machine-wide configuration, it could also be loaded in subsequent sessions, even after the developer moved to another directory. title: Stop building agents that can’t change models
summary: No one can predict which AI provider will win the next benchmark cycle. The smarter approach is to build an architecture that can adapt as models change. One with a stable contract between agents and models, tools and state that exist outside any single provider, and evaluations that make each model change a measurable decision. The goal isn’t to avoid choosing a preferred model. It’s to ensure that when the next model emerges, changing that choice doesn’t require rebuilding the system around it. For example, on June 15, 2026, Anthropic retired Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Opus 4 from its API, after giving developers notice on April 14. Any application still calling those model IDs started receiving errors. Claude Opus 4.1 followed on August 5. Later that month, OpenAI shut down its entire Assistants API and pointed developers to its Responses API. None of this was a surprise. Each provider published dates and migration guides well ahead of time. The problem sits on the builder’s side. Many teams designed agents where the model is the foundation and not a component, so when the foundation moves, the whole building moves with it. The model market is moving too fast for that design, and enterprises should treat models as replaceable compute behind stable interfaces. By doing so, they can change providers for cost, capability, privacy or performance without rebuilding their agents. The market refuses to sit still, and the rising costs of tokens According to Menlo Ventures , OpenAI held 50% of enterprise large language model (LLM) API usage in 2023. By the end of 2025, that share had fallen to 27%. Anthropic climbed from 12% to 40%, and Google went from 7% to 21%. The data clearly indicates that leadership in this market changes hands faster than most enterprise software contracts renew. title: How to make enterprise APIs agent-ready
summary: Enterprises spent the last decade building API programs. A large organization now runs thousands of internal APIs, each with a spec, owner, authentication scheme, and access policies enforced at a gateway. As agents move into production, those APIs are the obvious source of the context agents need: customer records, order status, inventory, pricing, and support tickets. The more difficult question now is how agents reach those systems at scale. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gave the industry a standard way to connect agents to tools. But the most common way teams expose APIs over MCP, one tool per API operation, starts to fail well before an agent touches a meaningful share of the enterprise’s API estate. Here’s why that happens, what a better pattern looks like, and how platform teams can build a context layer that reuses the governance they already have. Why one tool per endpoint doesn’t scale The default way to turn an API into an MCP server is to take its OpenAPI spec and generate one tool per operation. That works for a small API. However, a typical enterprise CRM or ERP API can have hundreds of operations, and an agent that needs a few of those APIs quickly faces hundreds of tool definitions. Using this approach, three things go sideways fast. Cost. Every tool definition loads into the model’s context before the agent does any work, and every intermediate result flows back through the model. A routine workflow, such as looking up a customer, pulling their open orders, and checking shipment status, pays for each hop in tokens. Accuracy. Once the tool list grows past what the model can reason about, tool selection degrades. The agent picks the wrong tool from a set of similar-looking options, or makes three calls where one would do. Latency. More context to process and more back-and-forth between the model and its tools slows the agent down. Users notice that long before anyone sees the token bill. title: Your npm install was safe. What happens when the package runs?
summary: For years, one of the first questions we asked about a suspicious npm package was whether it ran a pre-install or postinstall script. Those hooks can execute before a developer has written a line of code that uses the dependency. Blocking them is a sensible defense. It prevents a particular kind of package from running just because someone installed it. But installation is only the beginning of a package’s life in an application. Once that application starts, it calls the package’s functions with its own permissions, environment variables, network access, and data. A package can behave impeccably during installation and still become dangerous when the application uses it. That distinction is the lesson of the recently disclosed indexed-btree campaign . Checkmarx Zero found a malicious npm package that imitated the legitimate sorted-btree library. The package had no malicious install hook. Its loader sat inside BTree.prototype.set , a method the application would call as part of normal use. The reported trigger checked for a particular key value before launching an obfuscated file in a separate Node process. Merely installing the package did not trigger that behavior; neither would an import alone necessarily do so. The application had to reach the relevant method and condition. The precise key and second-stage machinery are useful to incident responders. The larger design failure is simpler: an install-time policy can tell us whether a package executed during installation. It cannot tell us whether code inside that package is safe to execute later. The wrong boundary When a team turns off life-cycle scripts, its installation process becomes safer in a specific, measurable way. npm’s ignore-scripts setting prevents scripts declared in package.json from running during installation. npm also offers controls for approving install-time scripts.
